Keep reasoning effort LOW — this is a fast reconnaissance pass, medium breadth. Repo: /home/diogenes/Projects/keating (an AI teaching app called Keating; a CLI/agent core in src/ and a web app in web/).

I'm designing a new "microworlds" feature: interactive, explorable mini-worlds the learner manipulates to learn by doing. It will likely be modeled on the existing "hyperframes" animation tool. I need a concise architectural overview of everything relevant. Please report:

1. The hyperframes animation pipeline end-to-end:
   - How the agent tool for animations is defined (look at src/pi/hyper-teacher/tools/teaching.ts, src/core/animation.ts, and anything else relevant)
   - What the animation payload/schema looks like (frames? scenes? timing?)
   - How it's rendered in the web UI (web/src/components/HyperframesPlayer.tsx — new untracked file, AnimationPlayer.tsx, AnimatedScene.tsx, animation-host.ts)
   - How the tool output travels from agent → chat message → rendered component (tag parsing? see web/src/test/interactive-tag-parsing.test.ts)

2. The interactive card pattern: how quiz/question/goal cards are emitted by tools, rendered, and how user interaction results flow back to the agent (window events, onNew, resultId feedback loop). Which files define this.

3. How agent tools are registered for the web agent (web/src/keating/browser-tools.ts) vs the CLI/pi agent (src/pi/hyper-teacher/), and whether there's shared code between them (shared/ directory?).

4. Any sandboxing/iframe/artifact-rendering infrastructure that already exists (ArtifactViewer.tsx, ArtifactBrowserOverlay.tsx, nodepod-boot-files.ts — what's a nodepod?). Can the web app already run arbitrary HTML/JS in a sandbox?

5. Where the system prompt / operational protocol describes when the agent should use animations (web/src/keating/prompts/operational-protocol.md), so I know where microworld guidance would go.

Report file paths with line numbers for the key integration points, the shape of the relevant schemas/types (paraphrased, not full dumps), and a short summary of how a new interactive tool would plug in. Keep the whole report under ~800 words.

content.text:
Confirmed: no shared code between `web/src/keating/browser-tools.ts` (self-contained web tool defs using `createTool`) and `src/pi/hyper-teacher/tools/*` (CLI, using `keatingToolMaker` from local `shared.ts`, calling into `src/core/*`). They're parallel, independently-maintained implementations of the same tool surface.

I have everything needed for the report.

## 1. Hyperframes pipeline

**Agent tool (web)** — `web/src/keating/browser-tools.ts:583-668`: `animate` tool. The model authors a *complete* HTML document with GSAP timelines itself (no server-side synthesis — a fallback path at line ~608 rejects short bodies and returns a worked example). Params: `topic`, `kind` (only `"hyperframes"` allowed), `summary`, `body` (required HTML), optional `storyboard`. It calls `storage.saveAnimation(...)` then emits a text reply containing `[artifact://animation/<id>]` followed by a `<keating-animation json="...">` tag whose JSON is `{topic, kind, summary, body}` (double-JSON-stringified).

**CLI/pi tool** — `src/pi/hyper-teacher/tools/teaching.ts:44-58` (`animate`) is a much thinner, non-authored version that calls `animateTopicArtifact` in `src/core/project.ts`, itself built on `src/core/animation.ts`, which defines `AnimationSceneKind` (function-graph, distribution-bars, belief-update, concept-card, code-trace, timeline, case-diagram, mind-map) and `AnimationManifest {topic, slug, domain, sceneKind, rationale, focusMoments}`. This CLI path is a template/manifest-driven storyboard generator — architecturally distinct from the web's "model authors raw HTML" approach. Treat the web path as the real precedent for microworlds.

**Payload shape**: `AnimationPayload` in `web/src/components/AnimatedScene.tsx:11-18` — `{topic: string, kind: "hyperframes", body?: string, summary?: string}`. No frame/scene array — the whole "scene" is one opaque HTML document; internal timing/sequencing is left to GSAP inside that document.

**Rendering**: `AnimatedScene.tsx` renders a header (topic/summary/badge) plus `AnimationBody`, which hands `body` to `HyperframesPlayer.tsx` (untracked, 161 lines). That component wraps the HTML via `buildHyperframesHtml()` in `animation-host.ts` (adds `<!doctype>`/chrome only if the model didn't already write one), turns it into a `Blob` URL, and loads it in `<iframe sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin" src={blobUrl}>`. Playback controls (play/pause/replay/scrub/loop) reach into the iframe's `contentWindow.gsap.globalTimeline` directly — a real cross-frame coupling to GSAP's API, not a message-passing protocol.

**Tag → component pipeline**: Tool output text (with the `<keating-animation json=...>` tag) becomes an assistant chat message. `web/src/components/AssistantChatPanel.tsx` has a generic tag scanner (`~line 1334`, regex covering `quiz|scene|question|goal|image|quiz-result|quiz-grade|animation|deck`) that calls `parseInteractiveSegments` (tested in `web/src/test/interactive-tag-parsing.test.ts`) to split message text into `{type, json}` segments, tolerant of `>`/`=>`/quotes inside the HTML body. Each segment is dispatched to a renderer switch (`~line 1531+`); the `"animation"` case calls `parseAnimationPayload` (in `AnimatedScene.tsx`) and renders `<AnimatedScene>`.

## 2. Interactive card pattern (quiz/goal) and feedback loop

Tools emit tags the same way (`<keating-quiz json=...>`, `<keating-goal json=...>`, etc). `AssistantChatPanel.tsx` renders quiz cards and wires their submit handlers to `window.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("keating:quiz-submitted", {...}))` (~line 1540) or `"keating:question-answered"` for ask-user-question. Panel-level `useEffect`s (~lines 3461-3600) listen for these window events, build a synthetic user message (sometimes with a generated `resultId`, e.g. `` `${quizId}-${Date.now()}` `` at line 3491) summarizing the interaction, and call `onNew(message)` (defined ~line 3359) to feed it back into the agent loop — this is the whole "UI action → new agent turn" round-trip. Grading results are additionally tracked via `QuizGradesContext` (`web/src/components/quiz-grades-context.tsx`) so `grade_quiz`/`quiz-grade` tags can update an existing card. `pendingQuizResults` (CLI-side, `src/pi/hyper-teacher/tools/shared.ts`) is the analogous in-process map for the terminal path, where grading happens synchronously via the `grade_quiz` tool rather than window events.

## 3. Tool registration: web vs CLI

`web/src/keating/browser-tools.ts` defines all web tools inline via a local `createTool(name, description, schema, handler)` helper — no shared module with the CLI. `src/pi/hyper-teacher/tools/*.ts` (teaching.ts, goals.ts, feedback.ts, ask-user-question.ts, self-evaluation.ts, self-evolution.ts) use `keatingToolMaker` from `src/pi/hyper-teacher/tools/shared.ts` and call into `src/core/*` business logic. There is no `shared/` directory linking web and pi — they are two independent tool implementations of overlapping concepts (quiz, goal, animate, etc.), and the web one is more advanced/authored while the CLI one is template-driven. A new microworld tool would need to be added twice, or you introduce a shared package.

## 4. Sandbox / arbitrary HTML-JS infrastructure

Yes — the hyperframes iframe (`sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin"`, blob-URL `src`) already executes arbitrary model-authored HTML/JS/CSS with no server round-trip. This is the direct precedent for microworlds: a sandboxed iframe fed a Blob URL. `ArtifactViewer.tsx`/`ArtifactBrowserOverlay.tsx` are a separate, older artifact-browsing UI (lesson plans, maps, animations, flashcards) built from `KeatingStorage` records — no additional sandboxing beyond reusing `AnimationPlayer`/`MermaidRenderer`. Separately, `web/src/keating/nodepod-runtime.ts` boots `@scelar/nodepod` (an in-browser Node.js-like VFS/runtime, "nodepod") seeded from `nodepod-boot-files.ts` (auto-generated from the CLI's prompt files) — this powers in-browser execution of the pi agent's own TypeScript/prompts (remote execution results), not user-facing sandboxed content; it's unrelated to iframe rendering.

## 5. Where to add microworld guidance

`web/src/keating/prompts/operational-protocol.md` — line 18 ("Call `map` or `animate` yourself when visual aids would help") and line 50 (tool reference: "`animate` — Save an animation you author yourself as `hyperframes` HTML..."). A microworlds tool description/usage guidance would sit alongside these two lines, likely as a new bullet analogous to line 50 plus a decision rule near line 18 for when to prefer an interactive microworld over a passive animation.

**Plug-in shape for a new tool**: define `microworld` in `browser-tools.ts` (schema forcing the model to author full HTML/JS, mirroring `animate`'s "no template fallback" pattern) → emit `<keating-microworld json=...>` → extend `parseInteractiveSegments`'s tag regex and switch in `AssistantChatPanel.tsx` → new `MicroworldScene`/`MicroworldPlayer` components modeled on `AnimatedScene`/`HyperframesPlayer`, reusing the same sandboxed-iframe-via-Blob-URL approach, but likely needing `postMessage` (rather than direct `gsap.globalTimeline` reach-in) for the learner-interaction feedback loop, dispatched as a new `keating:microworld-*` window event feeding back into `onNew`.

## 2. Interactive card pattern (quiz/goal) and feedback loop

Tools emit tags the same way (`<keating-quiz json=...>`, `<keating-goal json=...>`, etc). `AssistantChatPanel.tsx` renders quiz cards and wires their submit handlers to `window.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("keating:quiz-submitted", {...}))` (~line 1540) or `"keating:question-answered"` for ask-user-question. Panel-level `useEffect`s (~lines 3461-3600) listen for these window events, build a synthetic user message (sometimes with a generated `resultId`, e.g. `` `${quizId}-${Date.now()}` `` at line 3491) summarizing the interaction, and call `onNew(message)` (defined ~line 3359) to feed it back into the agent loop — this is the whole "UI action → new agent turn" round-trip. Grading results are additionally tracked via `QuizGradesContext` (`web/src/components/quiz-grades-context.tsx`) so `grade_quiz`/`quiz-grade` tags can update an existing card. `pendingQuizResults` (CLI-side, `src/pi/hyper-teacher/tools/shared.ts`) is the analogous in-process map for the terminal path, where grading happens synchronously via the `grade_quiz` tool rather than window events.

`web/src/keating/browser-tools.ts` defines all web tools inline via a local `createTool(name, description, schema, handler)` helper — no shared module with the CLI. `src/pi/hyper-teacher/tools/*.ts` (teaching.ts, goals.ts, feedback.ts, ask-user-question.ts, self-evaluation.ts, self-evolution.ts) use `keatingToolMaker` from `src/pi/hyper-teacher/tools/shared.ts` and call into `src/core/*` business logic. There is no `shared/` directory linking web and pi — they are two independent tool implementations of overlapping concepts (quiz, goal, animate, etc.), and the web one is more advanced/authored while the CLI one is template-driven. A new microworld tool would need to be added twice, or you introduce a shared package.

The explore agent came back with a clear picture, and the good news is that microworlds are a natural extension of what's already there. Here's the short version of the architecture, then my draft design.

**What exists:** the web `animate` tool has the model author a *complete* HTML+GSAP document, saves it, and emits a `<keating-animation json=...>` tag; `AssistantChatPanel` parses the tag and `HyperframesPlayer` runs the HTML in a sandboxed iframe via a blob URL. Separately, quiz/goal cards already have a full interaction loop: card UI → window `CustomEvent` → panel listener → synthetic user message via `onNew` → new agent turn, with `resultId` letting the agent update an already-rendered card. The web and CLI tool sets are parallel implementations with no shared package, and the web path is the more advanced one — so microworlds should be web-first.

## Draft: Microworlds in Keating

**Core idea.** A `microworld` tool that works like `animate` — the agent authors a self-contained HTML/JS world, no templates (consistent with your authored-artifacts rule) — but where hyperframes are *watched*, microworlds are *inhabited*. The one genuinely new piece is a two-way bridge so the learner's actions inside the iframe can reach the teacher, and the teacher can reach back into the running world. This is Papert's term, and it fits Keating's cognitive-empowerment thesis exactly: the learner learns by manipulating a world and forming theories, with the teacher watching and coaching rather than lecturing.

**The `window.keating` world API.** Instead of hyperframes' direct `contentWindow.gsap` reach-in, wrap the authored HTML (in a `buildMicroworldHtml`) with a tiny injected runtime the author codes against:

- `keating.milestone(id, data)` — a declared learning moment was hit ("landed the projectile in the bucket"). This is the main trigger for an agent turn.
- `keating.observe(event, data)` — lightweight action telemetry (slider moved, reset pressed), buffered, *not* triggering turns.
- `keating.ask(text)` — learner asks the teacher from inside the world; fires a turn with current state attached.
- `keating.registerState(fn)` — the world provides a serializer so a snapshot travels with every milestone/ask.
- `keating.onMessage(fn)` — the agent can push into a *running* world (change a parameter, add a challenge, drop a hint object into the scene).

Parent side, `MicroworldPlayer` translates postMessage ↔ window events (`keating:microworld-milestone` etc.), reusing the exact quiz-card feedback machinery. Bonus: with postMessage we can drop `allow-same-origin` from the sandbox — stricter isolation than hyperframes currently has.

**Tool schema.** Roughly: `topic`, `summary`, `body` (full HTML, required, rejected if thin — same guard as `animate`), plus `challenges: [{id, prompt}]`. Challenges render as a checklist *outside* the iframe on the card chrome; the world checks them off by calling `keating.milestone(challengeId)`. That gives every world a visible "what am I trying to do here" without constraining what's inside.

**Turn economics.** Don't fire an agent turn per click — buffer `observe` events and only go back to the agent on: milestone hit, explicit `ask`, or a "Show the teacher" button on the card that sends a state snapshot + recent event digest. This keeps the world feeling live without burning a model call on every slider twitch. A stuck-detection heuristic (N resets or M minutes with no milestone → digest to agent) could come later.

**Agent-side updates.** Mirror the `grade_quiz` → `quiz-grade` pattern: an `update_microworld` tool that targets a world by id and either pushes a message into the running iframe (`keating.onMessage`) or appends challenges. So the teacher can say "nice — now try it with gravity halved" and actually change the world mid-conversation.

**Example worlds** (all authorable as single HTML docs): projectile sandbox with a "land in the bucket" challenge; a Galton board where the challenge is "make the distribution skew left"; a grid-robot the learner programs with a tiny command palette; a two-good market where they chase equilibrium; a logic-gate breadboard.

**Phasing.**
1. **MVP:** `microworld` tool + tag parsing + `MicroworldPlayer` with the postMessage bridge, milestones, and challenge checklist. Plumbing is ~all cloned from `animate` + quiz cards. Add a decision rule to `operational-protocol.md` near the existing animate guidance: *animate to show, microworld to let them do.*
2. **Live coaching:** `update_microworld`, state snapshots persisted in storage so a learner can resume a world, artifact-browser entry.
3. **Constructionist endgame:** let the learner *edit* the world — "view source, change the rules" — which is the most Papert-faithful move and very on-brand for Keating.

The design questions I'd want your call on before speccing: whether milestones auto-trigger an agent turn or queue until the learner surfaces (auto feels magical but chatty); whether MVP includes `update_microworld` or ships read-only-teacher first; and whether CLI parity matters at all for this or it's web-only.
